1	# STATS 101 — Module 1: Data, Samples and Describing Data
2	
3	**Course:** STATS 101 (introductory, first-year undergraduate, no prior statistics)
4	**Class length:** 50 minutes
5	**Prerequisites:** high-school algebra
6	
7	## Learning objectives
8	
9	By the end of this module students can:
10	
11	1. Explain what statistics is for and tell a population from a sample, and a parameter from a statistic.
12	2. Classify variables (categorical or numerical) and their level of measurement.
13	3. Describe how data are collected (observational study or experiment, sampling methods) and spot common biases.
14	4. Choose a suitable graph for a variable.
15	5. Calculate and interpret measures of centre (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, IQR, standard deviation).
16	6. Find outliers with the 1.5 × IQR rule, compute z-scores and use the 68–95–99.7 rule.
17	7. Explain why correlation does not imply causation.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## 1. Why statistics?
22	
23	- Statistics is the science of **collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data** in the presence of variation and uncertainty.
24	- Two branches:
25	  - **Descriptive statistics** summarise the data we have (tables, graphs, averages). Most of this module.
26	  - **Inferential statistics** use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty. Later modules.
27	- Everyday examples: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, A/B tests on websites.
28	- The three questions that structure this module:
29	  1. **Where do the data come from?** (populations, samples, study design)
30	  2. **What kind of data are they?** (types of variables)
31	  3. **What do the data say?** (graphs, centre, spread, shape)
32	
33	## 2. Two stories about data
34	
35	**John Snow, London, 1854.** During a cholera outbreak in Soho, Snow marked each death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed. A simple picture of data pointed to the cause.
36	
37	**The Literary Digest poll, 1936.** The magazine mailed about 10 million ballots, drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists, and got about 2.4 million back. It predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin D. Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with about 61% of the popular vote and 46 of the 48 states. George Gallup, with a much smaller but better-chosen sample (about 50,000 people), correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.
38	
39	Takeaway: **a huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one.** How data are collected matters more than how much there is.
40	
41	## 3. Population, sample, parameter, statistic
42	
43	- **Population**: the entire group we want to know about (e.g. all students at the university).
44	- **Sample**: the part of the population we actually collect data from (e.g. 200 students who answered a survey).
45	- **Parameter**: a number describing the population (usually unknown). Notation: population mean **μ**, population standard deviation **σ**.
46	- **Statistic**: a number computed from the sample, used to estimate the parameter. Notation: sample mean **x̄**, sample standard deviation **s**.
47	- Memory aid: **P**opulation – **P**arameter; **S**ample – **S**tatistic.
48	
49	## 4. Types of variables
50	
51	| Type | Subtype | What it is | Examples |
52	|---|---|---|---|
53	| Categorical | Nominal | categories with no order | blood type, favourite colour, country |
54	| Categorical | Ordinal | categories with a natural order | satisfaction (low/medium/high), year of study |
55	| Numerical | Discrete | counts, whole numbers | number of siblings, goals scored |
56	| Numerical | Continuous | measurements on a scale | height, time, temperature |
57	
58	Watch out: numbers are not always numerical data. A postcode or a student ID is categorical; averaging them means nothing.
59	
60	## 5. Levels of measurement
61	
62	| Level | Order? | Equal intervals? | True zero? | Example |
63	|---|---|---|---|---|
64	| Nominal | no | no | no | eye colour |
65	| Ordinal | yes | no | no | race finishing position |
66	| Interval | yes | yes | no | temperature in °C |
67	| Ratio | yes | yes | yes | weight, income, time |
68	
69	Why it matters: 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C (interval, no true zero), but 20 kg is twice 10 kg (ratio).
70	
71	## 6. Collecting data: observational studies and experiments
72	
73	- **Observational study**: researchers observe and measure without assigning treatments (e.g. surveying students about sleep and grades). It can show an association, but not cause and effect.
74	- **Experiment**: researchers **assign** treatments and compare outcomes. Good experiments use:
75	  - a **control group** for comparison,
76	  - **random assignment** to groups, so the groups are alike apart from the treatment,
77	  - a **placebo** where possible, and **blinding** (double-blind: neither subjects nor researchers know who got what).
78	- Only a well-designed randomised experiment can establish **cause and effect**.
79	
80	## 7. Sampling methods
81	
82	| Method | How it works | Example |
83	|---|---|---|
84	| Simple random sample | every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen | draw 100 student IDs at random |
85	| Stratified sample | split into groups (strata), take a random sample from each | 25 students from each year of study |
86	| Cluster sample | split into groups, randomly choose whole groups | randomly pick 5 lecture sections, survey everyone in them |
87	| Systematic sample | choose every k-th individual from a list after a random start | every 20th name on the class list |
88	| Convenience sample | whoever is easiest to reach (**not random; avoid**) | asking friends in the cafeteria |
89	
90	## 8. Bias: when samples mislead
91	
92	- **Selection bias**: the way the sample is chosen leaves out part of the population (the Literary Digest's phone and car lists left out poorer voters in 1936).
93	- **Non-response bias**: the people who don't respond differ from those who do.
94	- **Response bias**: the question wording or setting pushes people towards an answer ("Don't you agree that…?").
95	- **Voluntary response bias**: only people with strong opinions choose to take part (online polls, call-in shows).
96	- A bigger sample does **not** fix bias; it only makes a biased answer look more precise.
97	
98	## 9. Graphs: picking the right one
99	
100	| Data | Graph | What it shows |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| One categorical variable | bar chart (or pie chart) | counts or percentages per category |
103	| One numerical variable | histogram | shape of the distribution |
104	| One numerical variable | box plot | five-number summary and outliers |
105	| Two numerical variables | scatter plot | relationship (direction, form, strength) |
106	| A variable over time | line graph | trends |
107	
108	Rule: **always plot the data before computing anything.**
109	
110	**Anscombe's quartet (1973):** four small data sets (11 points each) with almost the same mean of x (9), mean of y (about 7.50), correlation (about 0.816) and regression line (y = 3 + 0.5x), yet completely different scatter plots: one straight-line cloud, one curve, one line with a single outlier, one vertical stack with one far point. Summary numbers can hide the story.
111	
112	## 10. Describing a distribution: shape, centre, spread
113	
114	Every description of a numerical variable covers:
115	
116	- **Shape**: symmetric, skewed right (long tail to the right, e.g. incomes), skewed left; one peak (unimodal) or two (bimodal).
117	- **Centre**: where the typical value is.
118	- **Spread**: how much values vary.
119	- **Unusual features**: outliers, gaps.
120	
121	## 11. Measures of centre
122	
123	- **Mean**: add the values and divide by how many. x̄ = Σx / n
124	- **Median**: the middle value of the ordered data (average of the two middle values if n is even).
125	- **Mode**: the most frequent value.
126	
127	**Worked example.** Commute times (minutes) for 10 students:
128	
129	> 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 76
130	
131	- Sum = 260, n = 10 → **mean = 26 minutes**
132	- Ordered middle values are 20 and 22 → **median = 21 minutes**
133	- **Mode = 15 minutes** (appears twice)
134	
135	Remove the 76-minute commute: the mean drops to about **20.4**, the median only to **20**.
136	
137	- The median is **resistant** to outliers; the mean is not.
138	- In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled above the median (mean > median); in a left-skewed one, below.
139	- Use the median for skewed data (house prices, incomes); the mean for roughly symmetric data.
140	
141	## 12. Measures of spread
142	
143	- **Range** = maximum − minimum. Commute example: 76 − 12 = **64 minutes**. Very sensitive to outliers.
144	- **Quartiles**: Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q3 the median of the upper half.
145	  Commute example: lower half 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 → **Q1 = 15**; upper half 22, 25, 27, 30, 76 → **Q3 = 27**.
146	- **Interquartile range (IQR)** = Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 15 = **12 minutes**: the spread of the middle 50%.
147	- **Standard deviation (s)**: roughly the typical distance of values from the mean.
148	
149	> s = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) )
150	
151	  Commute example: variance ≈ 341.3, **s ≈ 18.5 minutes**. Without the 76-minute value, s ≈ 6.1: one outlier triples the SD.
152	- We divide by n − 1 (not n) for a sample; this corrects for the sample mean being closer to the data than the true mean.
153	
154	## 13. The five-number summary, box plots and outliers
155	
156	- **Five-number summary**: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
157	  Commute example: 12, 15, 21, 27, 76.
158	- **1.5 × IQR rule** for outliers: a value is a suspected outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
159	  Commute example: 1.5 × 12 = 18; fences are 15 − 18 = **−3** and 27 + 18 = **45**. The **76-minute commute is an outlier**.
160	- A **box plot** draws the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values that are not outliers (here 12 and 30), and outliers as separate dots (here 76).
161	
162	## 14. z-scores: how unusual is a value?
163	
164	> z = (x − mean) / standard deviation
165	
166	- A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is above (+) or below (−) the mean.
167	- Example: an exam has mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = **2**: two SDs above the mean.
168	- z-scores let us compare values on different scales (e.g. a score on a hard test vs an easy one).
169	
170	## 15. The 68–95–99.7 rule
171	
172	For data with a roughly **normal (bell-shaped)** distribution:
173	
174	- about **68%** of values lie within 1 SD of the mean,
175	- about **95%** within 2 SDs,
176	- about **99.7%** within 3 SDs.
177	
178	Exam example (mean 70, SD 8): about 68% of scores between **62 and 78**, about 95% between **54 and 86**, about 99.7% between **46 and 94**. A score of 86 (z = 2) is better than about 97.5% of the class.
179	
180	The rule only applies to roughly bell-shaped data; it does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.
181	
182	## 16. Correlation is not causation
183	
184	- Two variables are **associated** (correlated) when they tend to move together.
185	- Classic example: across a year, **ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together**. Ice cream does not cause drowning; **hot weather** drives both. Hot weather is a **confounding variable**.
186	- Other reasons for a correlation without causation: reverse causation, coincidence (especially when many variables are searched).
187	- Only a randomised experiment (Section 6) can show cause and effect.
188	
189	## 17. Summary
190	
191	1. Statistics turns data into conclusions in the presence of variation.
192	2. Population → parameter (μ, σ); sample → statistic (x̄, s).
193	3. Variables are categorical (nominal, ordinal) or numerical (discrete, continuous).
194	4. How data are collected matters most: random sampling and randomised experiments; bigger biased samples do not help (Literary Digest 1936).
195	5. Always plot first (Anscombe's quartet).
196	6. Centre: mean (sensitive) vs median (resistant). Spread: range, IQR, SD.
197	7. Outliers: beyond Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
198	8. z = (x − mean) / SD; for bell-shaped data, 68–95–99.7.
199	9. Correlation is not causation; look for confounders.
200	
201	**Next module (Module 2):** Probability — the language of uncertainty.
202	
203	## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)
204	
205	1. Is "favourite colour" categorical or numerical, and at what level? *(Answer: categorical, nominal)*
206	2. A survey about exercise habits only asks people leaving a gym. What is the problem? *(Answer: selection bias from a convenience sample; gym-goers exercise more than the population)*
207	3. Find the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10. *(Answer: mean 5, median 4)*
208	4. Which is resistant to outliers: the mean or the median? *(Answer: the median)*
209	5. An exam has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of 82? *(Answer: 1.5)*
210	6. Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated. Does ice cream cause drowning? *(Answer: no; hot weather is a confounding variable)*
211	
212	## Glossary
213	
214	- **Bias** — a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth in one direction.
215	- **Confounding variable** — a third variable that affects both variables being studied.
216	- **IQR** — interquartile range, Q3 − Q1.
217	- **Outlier** — a value far from the rest of the data.
218	- **Parameter** — a number describing a population.
219	- **Statistic** — a number computed from a sample.
220	- **Standard deviation** — a measure of the typical distance of values from the mean.
221	- **z-score** — the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean.

# STATS 101 — Module 1: Data, Samples and Describing Data

**Class length:** 50 minutes
**Prerequisites:** high-school algebra

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module students can:

1. Explain what statistics is for and tell a population from a sample, and a parameter from a statistic.
2. Classify variables (categorical or numerical) and their level of measurement.
3. Describe how data are collected (observational study or experiment, sampling methods) and spot common biases.
4. Choose a suitable graph for a variable.
5. Calculate and interpret measures of centre (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, IQR, standard deviation).
6. Find outliers with the 1.5 × IQR rule, compute z-scores and use the 68–95–99.7 rule.
7. Explain why correlation does not imply causation.

---

## 1. Why statistics?

- Statistics is the science of **collecting, describing and drawing conclusions from data** in the presence of variation and uncertainty.
- Two branches:

  - **Inferential statistics** use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, with a measure of uncertainty. Later modules.
- Everyday examples: opinion polls, clinical trials of new medicines, sports analytics, weather forecasts, A/B tests on websites.

  1. **Where do the data come from?** (populations, samples, study design)
  2. **What kind of data are they?** (types of variables)
  3. **What do the data say?** (graphs, centre, spread, shape)

## 2. Two stories about data

**John Snow, London, 1854.** During a cholera outbreak in Soho, Snow marked each death on a street map. The deaths clustered around one water pump on Broad Street. The pump's handle was removed. A simple picture of data pointed to the cause.

**The Literary Digest poll, 1936.** The magazine mailed about 10 million ballots, drawn largely from telephone directories and car-registration lists, and got about 2.4 million back. It predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin D. Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with about 61% of the popular vote and 46 of the 48 states. George Gallup, with a much smaller but better-chosen sample (about 50,000 people), correctly predicted Roosevelt's win.

Takeaway: **a huge biased sample is worse than a small well-chosen one.** How data are collected matters more than how much there is.

## 3. Population, sample, parameter, statistic

- **Population**: the entire group we want to know about (e.g. all students at the university).
- **Sample**: the part of the population we actually collect data from (e.g. 200 students who answered a survey).
- **Parameter**: a number describing the population (usually unknown). Notation: population mean **μ**, population standard deviation **σ**.
- **Statistic**: a number computed from the sample, used to estimate the parameter. Notation: sample mean **x̄**, sample standard deviation **s**.
- Memory aid: **P**opulation – **P**arameter; **S**ample – **S**tatistic.

## 4. Types of variables

| Type | Subtype | What it is | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Categorical | Nominal | categories with no order | blood type, favourite colour, country |
| Categorical | Ordinal | categories with a natural order | satisfaction (low/medium/high), year of study |
| Numerical | Discrete | counts, whole numbers | number of siblings, goals scored |
| Numerical | Continuous | measurements on a scale | height, time, temperature |

Watch out: numbers are not always numerical data. A postcode or a student ID is categorical; averaging them means nothing.

## 5. Levels of measurement

| Level | Order? | Equal intervals? | True zero? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominal | no | no | no | eye colour |
| Ordinal | yes | no | no | race finishing position |
| Interval | yes | yes | no | temperature in °C |
| Ratio | yes | yes | yes | weight, income, time |

Why it matters: 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C (interval, no true zero), but 20 kg is twice 10 kg (ratio).

## 6. Collecting data: observational studies and experiments

- **Observational study**: researchers observe and measure without assigning treatments (e.g. surveying students about sleep and grades). It can show an association, but not cause and effect.
- **Experiment**: researchers **assign** treatments and compare outcomes. Good experiments use:
  - a **control group** for comparison,
  - **random assignment** to groups, so the groups are alike apart from the treatment,
  - a **placebo** where possible, and **blinding** (double-blind: neither subjects nor researchers know who got what).
- Only a well-designed randomised experiment can establish **cause and effect**.

## 7. Sampling methods

| Method | How it works | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Simple random sample | every group of n individuals has the same chance of being chosen | draw 100 student IDs at random |
| Stratified sample | split into groups (strata), take a random sample from each | 25 students from each year of study |
| Cluster sample | split into groups, randomly choose whole groups | randomly pick 5 lecture sections, survey everyone in them |
| Systematic sample | choose every k-th individual from a list after a random start | every 20th name on the class list |
| Convenience sample | whoever is easiest to reach (**not random; avoid**) | asking friends in the cafeteria |

## 8. Bias: when samples mislead

- **Selection bias**: the way the sample is chosen leaves out part of the population (the Literary Digest's phone and car lists left out poorer voters in 1936).
- **Non-response bias**: the people who don't respond differ from those who do.
- **Response bias**: the question wording or setting pushes people towards an answer ("Don't you agree that…?").
- **Voluntary response bias**: only people with strong opinions choose to take part (online polls, call-in shows).
- A bigger sample does **not** fix bias; it only makes a biased answer look more precise.

## 9. Graphs: picking the right one

| Data | Graph | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| One categorical variable | bar chart (or pie chart) | counts or percentages per category |
| One numerical variable | histogram | shape of the distribution |
| One numerical variable | box plot | five-number summary and outliers |
| Two numerical variables | scatter plot | relationship (direction, form, strength) |
| A variable over time | line graph | trends |

Rule: **always plot the data before computing anything.**

**Anscombe's quartet (1973):** four small data sets (11 points each) with almost the same mean of x (9), mean of y (about 7.50), correlation (about 0.816) and regression line (y = 3 + 0.5x), yet completely different scatter plots: one straight-line cloud, one curve, one line with a single outlier, one vertical stack with one far point. Summary numbers can hide the story.

## 10. Describing a distribution: shape, centre, spread

Every description of a numerical variable covers:

- **Shape**: symmetric, skewed right (long tail to the right, e.g. incomes), skewed left; one peak (unimodal) or two (bimodal).
- **Centre**: where the typical value is.
- **Spread**: how much values vary.
- **Unusual features**: outliers, gaps.

## 11. Measures of centre

- **Mean**: add the values and divide by how many. x̄ = Σx / n
- **Median**: the middle value of the ordered data (average of the two middle values if n is even).
- **Mode**: the most frequent value.

**Worked example.** Commute times (minutes) for 10 students:

> 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, 76

- Sum = 260, n = 10 → **mean = 26 minutes**
- Ordered middle values are 20 and 22 → **median = 21 minutes**
- **Mode = 15 minutes** (appears twice)

Remove the 76-minute commute: the mean drops to about **20.4**, the median only to **20**.

- The median is **resistant** to outliers; the mean is not.
- In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled above the median (mean > median); in a left-skewed one, below.
- Use the median for skewed data (house prices, incomes); the mean for roughly symmetric data.

## 12. Measures of spread

- **Range** = maximum − minimum. Commute example: 76 − 12 = **64 minutes**. Very sensitive to outliers.
- **Quartiles**: Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q3 the median of the upper half.
  Commute example: lower half 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 → **Q1 = 15**; upper half 22, 25, 27, 30, 76 → **Q3 = 27**.
- **Interquartile range (IQR)** = Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 15 = **12 minutes**: the spread of the middle 50%.
- **Standard deviation (s)**: roughly the typical distance of values from the mean.

> s = √( Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) )

  Commute example: variance ≈ 341.3, **s ≈ 18.5 minutes**. Without the 76-minute value, s ≈ 6.1: one outlier triples the SD.
- We divide by n − 1 (not n) for a sample; this corrects for the sample mean being closer to the data than the true mean.

## 13. The five-number summary, box plots and outliers

- **Five-number summary**: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
  Commute example: 12, 15, 21, 27, 76.
- **1.5 × IQR rule** for outliers: a value is a suspected outlier if it is below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
  Commute example: 1.5 × 12 = 18; fences are 15 − 18 = **−3** and 27 + 18 = **45**. The **76-minute commute is an outlier**.
- A **box plot** draws the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values that are not outliers (here 12 and 30), and outliers as separate dots (here 76).

## 14. z-scores: how unusual is a value?

> z = (x − mean) / standard deviation

- A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is above (+) or below (−) the mean.
- Example: an exam has mean 70 and SD 8. A score of 86 has z = (86 − 70) / 8 = **2**: two SDs above the mean.
- z-scores let us compare values on different scales (e.g. a score on a hard test vs an easy one).

## 15. The 68–95–99.7 rule

For data with a roughly **normal (bell-shaped)** distribution:

- about **68%** of values lie within 1 SD of the mean,
- about **95%** within 2 SDs,
- about **99.7%** within 3 SDs.

Exam example (mean 70, SD 8): about 68% of scores between **62 and 78**, about 95% between **54 and 86**, about 99.7% between **46 and 94**. A score of 86 (z = 2) is better than about 97.5% of the class.

The rule only applies to roughly bell-shaped data; it does not apply to strongly skewed data like the commute times.

## 16. Correlation is not causation

- Two variables are **associated** (correlated) when they tend to move together.
- Classic example: across a year, **ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together**. Ice cream does not cause drowning; **hot weather** drives both. Hot weather is a **confounding variable**.
- Other reasons for a correlation without causation: reverse causation, coincidence (especially when many variables are searched).
- Only a randomised experiment (Section 6) can show cause and effect.

## 17. Summary

1. Statistics turns data into conclusions in the presence of variation.
2. Population → parameter (μ, σ); sample → statistic (x̄, s).
3. Variables are categorical (nominal, ordinal) or numerical (discrete, continuous).
4. How data are collected matters most: random sampling and randomised experiments; bigger biased samples do not help (Literary Digest 1936).
5. Always plot first (Anscombe's quartet).
6. Centre: mean (sensitive) vs median (resistant). Spread: range, IQR, SD.
7. Outliers: beyond Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
8. z = (x − mean) / SD; for bell-shaped data, 68–95–99.7.
9. Correlation is not causation; look for confounders.

**Next module (Module 2):** Probability — the language of uncertainty.

## 18. Check your understanding (quiz)

1. Is "favourite colour" categorical or numerical, and at what level? *(Answer: categorical, nominal)*
2. A survey about exercise habits only asks people leaving a gym. What is the problem? *(Answer: selection bias from a convenience sample; gym-goers exercise more than the population)*
3. Find the mean and median of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10. *(Answer: mean 5, median 4)*
4. Which is resistant to outliers: the mean or the median? *(Answer: the median)*
5. An exam has mean 70 and SD 8. What is the z-score of 82? *(Answer: 1.5)*
6. Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated. Does ice cream cause drowning? *(Answer: no; hot weather is a confounding variable)*

## Glossary

- **Bias** — a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth in one direction.
- **Confounding variable** — a third variable that affects both variables being studied.
- **IQR** — interquartile range, Q3 − Q1.
- **Outlier** — a value far from the rest of the data.
- **Parameter** — a number describing a population.
- **Statistic** — a number computed from a sample.
- **Standard deviation** — a measure of the typical distance of values from the mean.
- **z-score** — the number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean.

# The outline (PLAN.md)

The contract between planning and building. Whoever builds the deck follows it slide by slide, and the review compares the
finished deck against it, so every field is concrete: no "TBD" except facts the user still has to supply.

## Format

```markdown
# <Deck title>

- **Audience**: who, and what they already know
- **Occasion and time**: event, slot in minutes, whether Q&A is inside the slot
- **Goal**: what the audience should know, decide or do at the end
- **Promise**: By the end you will ... (said on slide 1 or 2)
- **Story**: the whole argument in one sentence
- **Fence**: what the idea is not (the nearest alternative it could be confused with)
- **Look**: data-theme, data-fonts (empty = the theme's own), lang/dir, one line on why
- **Sources**: each file or link used, one per line
- **Placeholders**: facts still missing, or "none"

| # | data-id | layout | claim (the slide's h2) | content and facts (with source) | role | min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | start | title | ... | subtitle = the promise | promise | 0.5 |
| 2 | agenda | agenda | ... | the parts | signpost | 0.5 |
| ... |
| n | close | closing | ... | what the audience now has, or the ask | contribution | 1 |

**Total**: n slides, about N minutes (finish at 85 to 90% of the slot when Q&A is inside it).
**Restatements of the story**: slides a, b, c (three, said three different ways).
```

## Rules for filling it in

- **Claim**: a sentence that states something ("Revenue grew 18%"), not a topic ("Revenue"). The titles alone, read in
  order, tell the story.
- **Content and facts**: only from the user's material, each with its source; anything missing is a named placeholder.
- **Role**, one or more per slide: promise, signpost, thesis (a restatement of the story), fence, evidence, story (an
  example or case that makes a number tangible), question (to the room), contribution, backup.
- **Layout**: one from `references/looks.md`; no more than two bullet slides in a row.
- **Minutes**: about one per slide for a talk, 1.5 to 2 for a lecture; the total fits the slot.
- **Required roles**: a promise in slides 1 to 2, the story restated three times, a fence, a contribution or the ask
  as the last slide (never "Thank you" or "Questions?"), and signposts when the talk is longer than about 10 minutes.
- Backup slides go last with role `backup`; they start with an appendix slide and are not counted in the time.

Add `<aside class="notes"><p>...</p></aside>` inside any slide for presenter notes. 27 4. `node check.mjs my-deck.html`, fix what it lists, open it, press **P**. 28 29 Rules of thumb: one idea per slide; at most 5 bullets; say the number, not the paragraph. Layouts auto-fit 30 (type shrinks to 78% before content would leave the safe area, and short content grows, up to 1.25x on bullets and 1.5x on statements, so a slide is never half empty), lists balance their wrapping, images crop with 31 `object-fit: cover`. You never tune CSS to make text fit; if `check.mjs` still complains, cut words. 32 33 ## 2. Layout cheat-sheet (shortest working snippet for each) 34 35 Every snippet goes inside `<section class="slide" data-layout="NAME"> ... </section>`. Optional extras are in comments. 36 37 ```html 38 <!-- title --> <h1>Title with <em>one accent</em></h1><p class="sub">Subtitle</p> 39 <!-- <p class="label">Event</p> <p class="meta"><span>Name</span><span>Date</span></p> --> 40 <!-- section --> <h2>Part two</h2> <!-- <p class="label">Part two</p> <span class="num">2</span> <p>One-line promise</p> --> 41 <!-- statement --> <h2>One huge sentence with an <em>accent</em>.</h2> 42 <!-- agenda --> <h2>Agenda</h2><ol><li>Results <small>10 min</small></li><li>Plan</li></ol> <!-- aria-current on an li dims the rest --> 43 <!-- bullets --> <h2>Title</h2><ul data-build="list"><li><strong>Lead.</strong> Support.</li><li>Two</li><li>Three</li></ul> 44 <!-- two-column --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="col"><h3>A</h3><p>Text</p></div><div class="col"><h3>B</h3><ul><li>x</li></ul></div> 45 <!-- image-left --> <figure><img src="a.jpg" alt=""></figure><h2>Title</h2><p>Text</p> <!-- empty <figure></figure> = placeholder art --> 46 <!-- image-right --> (same markup, mirrored) 47 <!-- full-bleed --> <h2>Title on a photo</h2> <!-- data-bg="photo.jpg" on the section, or <img class="bleed" src alt=""> --> 48 <!-- big-number --> <div class="big" data-build="count">98<small>%</small></div><p>One honest caption.</p> <!-- <p class="src">Source</p> --> 49 <!-- stats --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="stat"><b>4.2M</b><span>Users</span></div> ...2 to 4 of these 50 <!-- chart --> <h2>Title</h2><p class="lede">Takeaway</p> 51 <figure class="chart" data-chart="column" data-values="Q1:12,Q2:18,Q3:21"></figure> 52 <!-- data-chart: column | bar | line. Multi-series: put a <table> inside (header row + label column). 53 data-prefix="$" data-unit="M" data-decimals="1" data-highlight="3" (1-based or a label) 54 data-min="92" (line charts only) data-build="draw" (bars grow, lines draw) 55 data-wide on the section = full-width plot; <figcaption>Source</figcaption> --> 56 <!-- comparison --> <h2>Title</h2><table><thead><tr><th></th><th>A</th><th class="rec" data-tag="Recommended">B</th></tr></thead> 57 <tbody><tr><th>Price</th><td>$1</td><td>$2</td></tr></tbody></table> 58 <!-- timeline --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="timeline" data-build="list"><li><time>Q1</time><h3>Step</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- class="now" marks today --> 59 <!-- process --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="steps" data-build="list"><li><h3>Capture</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- 3 to 5 steps --> 60 <!-- quote --> <blockquote>The quote with an <em>accent</em>.</blockquote><cite><b>Name</b>Title, Company</cite> 61 <!-- code --> <h2>Title</h2><pre data-lang="js" data-focus="1-2;4-6;*"> code </pre> <!-- indent freely; focus steps light lines per click --> 62 <!-- team --> <h2>Team</h2><div class="people"><figure class="person" data-initials="AK"><figcaption><b>Ann</b><span>Role</span></figcaption></figure>...</div> 63 <!-- diagram --> <h2>Title</h2><figure class="dg"><svg viewBox="0 0 1680 400">...</svg></figure> <!-- see Diagrams --> 64 <!-- case --> <p class="label">Case</p><h2>Title</h2><div class="pt"><h3>History</h3><p>Summary</p></div> 65 <div class="vitals"><div class="vital" data-flag="high"><span>BP</span><b>162/94</b></div><div class="vital"><span>HR</span><b>96</b></div></div> 66 <ol class="course" data-build="list"><li><time>00:06</time>Event</li></ol> <!-- summary left; 2 to 4 vitals; timed course. data-flag marks an abnormal value --> 67 <!-- ask --> <h2>Raising a seed round</h2><div class="amount"><b data-build="count">$2.5<small>M</small></b><span>What it buys</span></div> 68 <ul class="use"><li style="--w:50"><b>Engineering</b><span>50%</span><i></i></li></ul><dl class="terms"><div><dt>Instrument</dt><dd>SAFE</dd></div></dl> 69 <!-- rows --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="rows"><li data-k="Issue"><p>Text</p></li><li data-k="Conclusion" data-hot><h3>Bold line</h3><p>Text</p></li></ol> 70 <!-- labelled rows: issue / rule / application / conclusion; situation / complication / resolution; claim / evidence / caveat. data-hot highlights one --> 71 <!-- quiz --> <h2>Question?</h2><ol class="opts" data-build="reveal"><li>A</li><li data-correct>B</li><li>C</li><li>D</li></ol> <!-- the click marks the data-correct option --> 72 <!-- materials --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="board"><figure class="mat" style="--sw:#9a9892"><figcaption><b>Concrete</b><span>Where it goes</span></figcaption></figure>...</div> <!-- or an <img> in each figure; --tx adds a texture gradient --> 73 <!-- formula --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="eq"><i>P<sub>r</sub></i> = <i>P<sub>t</sub></i> − <span class="hot"><i>L</i></span></div><dl class="terms"><div><dt><i>P<sub>t</sub></i></dt><dd>Meaning</dd></div></dl> 74 <!-- two-column x3 -> add data-cols="3" to the section for three columns (now / next / later) --> 75 <!-- closing --> <h2>Thank you</h2><p class="contact"><span><b>Web</b> example.com</span><span>me@example.com</span></p> 76 ``` 77 78 Extras: `<p class="label">` is the small mono kicker above a title (use it on some slides, not all). `.chip` is a boxed token; `.chip.hot` 79 highlights one. `.lede`, `.src` and `<small>` are secondary text. `data-footer="off"` hides the footer, `data-fit="off"` stops auto-fit, 80 `data-tone="hero"` (or `"plain"`) swaps a slide into (or out of) the theme's hero palette. 81 82 ## 3. Deck recipes (theme, fonts, sequence, builds) 83 84 Fonts: `data-fonts` is optional; leave it empty to use the theme's own pairing. 85 86 | Need | Theme | Sequence of layouts | Builds | 87 |---|---|---|---| 88 | **Product launch** | `keynote-black` (cinematic) or `keynote-white` | title, statement, statement + big-number (Magic Move on the number), stats, full-bleed, image-left, chart or comparison, quote, timeline, closing | `count` on stats, `list` on timeline, magic on the hero number | 89 | **Quarterly / board review** | `boardroom` | title, agenda, big-number, chart (actual vs plan), stats, chart (line with `data-min`), section, comparison (mark `rec`), two-column (risks / mitigations), timeline, bullets (decisions), closing | `count` on KPIs, `draw` on charts, `list` on decisions | 90 | **Tech talk** | `swiss` (or `studio`) | title, statement + big-number (problem), diagram (before), section, diagram (after), process, code (`data-focus`), chart (line), comparison, two-column (worked / didn't), stats, closing | `draw` + `fade` on diagram groups, focus on code | 91 | **Training / course** | `studio` (or `editorial`) | title, agenda, statement, diagrams, process, big-number, chart, comparison, code, quote, timeline (where we are), closing | `list`, `draw`, one `count` | 92 | **Investor pitch** | `keynote-white` + `data-fonts="grotesk"` | title, statement (problem), big-number (market), image-left (solution), stats (traction), chart (growth), comparison (vs alternatives), team, timeline (use of funds), closing | `count` on traction, `draw` on the growth chart | 93 | **Weekly status update** | `editorial` or `keynote-white` | title, bullets (done), stats (health), chart (trend), timeline (next), two-column (risks / asks), closing | `list` only; keep it quiet | 94 95 Authoring order that works in one pass: write the title and the one-sentence story, pick the recipe, write each slide's single 96 claim as its `<h2>`, then add the supporting snippet, then notes, then run `check.mjs`. 97 98 ## 4. Theme design plans (DESIGN.md format) 99 100 Each theme is a real, shippable look. One accent, hairline rules, big type. All body text is at least 4.5:1. 101 102 ### keynote-white 103 - **Overview.** Apple-clean. Mostly white, enormous tightly-tracked headlines, one blue phrase per slide. Fits launches, pitches, status decks. 104 - **Colors.** bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f5f5f7`, ink `#1d1d1f`, ink2 `#5f5f64`, rule `#d2d2d7`, brand `#0066cc` (on-brand `#fff`), hero = same as page. 105 - **Typography.** Display and body Inter (700 display, -0.035em), mono JetBrains Mono for labels and code. 106 - **Shape.** Radius 14 px (panels), 6 px bars, 1 px rules. 107 - **Signature.** Whitespace and scale; the accent `<em>` is the only colour on a title. 108 - **Do / Don't.** Do keep slides sparse. Don't add boxes around everything. 109 110 ### keynote-black 111 - **Overview.** Cinematic dark for reveals and demos; the same system on pure black. 112 - **Colors.** bg `#000`, surface `#161618`, ink `#f5f5f7`, ink2 `#a1a1a6`, rule `#38383a`, brand `#2997ff`, em gradient `#2997ff` to `#c58bff`. 113 - **Typography.** Inter 700 display; JetBrains Mono. 114 - **Shape.** 14 px radius, 6 px bars. 115 - **Signature.** Gradient-filled headline accent, the only gradient in the system. Code panel `#1c1c1e` with Xcode-dark colours. 116 - **Do / Don't.** Do use for rooms with dim light. Don't print it (use keynote-white for PDF handouts). 117 118 ### boardroom 119 - **Overview.** PowerPoint-corporate done well: navy, serif titles, gold accent, rules above the footer. 120 - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#eef1f6`, ink `#0b2545`, ink2 `#46576f`, rule `#c8d0dc`, brand `#c19a3d` (text version `#7a5a0a`); hero bg navy `#0b2545` with gold `#e2b658`. 121 - **Typography.** Source Serif 4 (600) titles, Source Sans 3 body, JetBrains Mono. 122 - **Shape.** 2 px radius, square bars, 1 px rules. 123 - **Signature.** Gold spine on title and closing slides; gold left bar on every title; navy code panel. 124 - **Do / Don't.** Do put the decision on the last slide. Don't use more than one chart per slide. 125 126 ### swiss 127 - **Overview.** International typographic style: hard grid, black rules, one red. 128 - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#f0f0f0`, ink `#111`, ink2 `#555`, rule `#cfcfcf`, strong rule `#111`, brand `#d7000f`; hero slides are solid red with white type. 129 - **Typography.** Inter Tight 700 (-0.03em) display, Inter body, JetBrains Mono. 130 - **Shape.** Zero radius everywhere, 2 px black rule above the footer. 131 - **Signature.** A 96x20 red tab on the top margin and full-red hero slides. 132 - **Do / Don't.** Do align everything to the grid. Don't round corners. 133 134 ### editorial 135 - **Overview.** A printed essay: paper, ink, oxblood, italic emphasis. 136 - **Colors.** bg `#f4efe6`, surface `#ebe4d6`, ink `#1c1a17`, ink2 `#5a5347`, rule `#cfc5b2`, brand `#8f2d17`; hero is ink `#1c1a17` with terracotta `#e49467`. 137 - **Typography.** Newsreader 400 display (italic for `<em>`), Inter body, JetBrains Mono. 138 - **Shape.** Zero radius, 1 px rules. 139 - **Signature.** A masthead double rule across the top of every slide. 140 - **Do / Don't.** Do write full sentences as titles. Don't use all-caps. 141 142 ### studio 143 - **Overview.** Deep teal and amber, the look of the Wireless 101 courses: for teaching and talks. 144 - **Colors.** bg `#0a2a2f`, surface `#0f3a40`, ink `#efe8d8`, ink2 `#a9c0bd`, rule `#2c5a5f`, brand `#f0a93b` (on-brand `#0a2a2f`); hero `#061c20`. 145 - **Typography.** Instrument Serif display (italic amber `<em>`), DM Sans body, Space Mono labels. 146 - **Shape.** 4 px radius, 2 px bars. 147 - **Signature.** An amber dot starts every label. 148 - **Do / Don't.** Do keep diagrams to the amber and cream. Don't add a second accent. 149 150 Press **S** in any deck to switch theme and font pairing live; hovering an option previews it on the slide, a click keeps it (remembered per deck in localStorage). 151 152 **Font library** (9 core pairings below live in the template; the profession pairings live in `library/fonts/` and are copied into a deck with `tools/add-look.mjs`. The settings panel groups them as Core and Library, and picking a library theme selects its own pairing; `fonts.html` shows them all as specimens with your own headline): Inter (neo-grotesk), Sora/Inter (geometric), Space Grotesk/Inter (grotesk with character), IBM Plex Sans/Plex Mono (technical), Fraunces/Inter, Playfair/Source Sans, 153 Spectral/Public Sans, Cormorant Garamond/Source Sans (set at 1.15x via `--display-scale`), and system fonts. Type sizes come from one scale: `--t-display --t-h1 --t-h2 --t-h3 --t-body --t-small` (164/132/84/48/36/28 px; 28 px is the floor for anything the audience reads). 154 Set one with `data-fonts="sora"` on `<html>`. To recolour any theme, add one line: `html{--brand:#7c3aed;--brand-text:#7c3aed}`. 155 156 ## 5. Builds, transitions, Magic Move 157 158 **Builds** reveal parts of a slide one click at a time. Right arrow / space / click reveals the next build, then the next slide; left steps back. 159 160 | Attribute | Effect | 161 |---|---| 162 | `data-build="fade"`, `rise`, `scale`, `wipe` | the element appears | 163 | `data-build="list"` on a `ul`/`ol` | children appear one by one (`data-item="fade"` to change the style) | 164 | `data-build="draw"` on an SVG shape or `<g>` | strokes draw themselves (every shape inside is staggered) | 165 | `data-build="count"` | the number counts up from 0 (`$4.2M`, `38.4%`, `1,840` all work); markup holds the final value | 166 | `data-build="draw"` on a chart figure | bars grow, lines draw, labels arrive | 167 | `data-focus="1-3;5-7;*"` on a `pre` | each click lights the next range of lines (`*` = all) | 168 | `data-order="2"` | builds with the same order arrive together; give all builds an order or none | 169 | `data-delay="200"` | extra delay in ms | 170 171 Print, overview thumbnails and `check.mjs` always show every build; the presenter window's Next pane shows the next one. Charts take `data-target="200"` (a dashed target line), `data-delta="pct"` or `"abs"` (a delta label on two-series columns), `data-muted="2"` (which series is the muted reference; with two bar series the second is one by default, `data-equal` turns that off) and `data-highlight` (also on line charts). Chart data is exposed to screen readers as a hidden table. Use builds where order matters; most slides need none. 172 173 **Skip, appendix and the end.** `data-skip` on a slide keeps it in the overview, outline and PDF but jumps over it in play (Keynote's Skip Slide); use it for backup slides. A slide with `data-layout="appendix"` renders as a section divider and it and every slide after it are skipped in play. Pressing next on the last slide shows an "End of show" screen (`data-end="off"` on the deck turns it off). Cite sources with `<sup class="cite">[1]</sup>` and list them on a `references` slide (`<ol class="refs"><li><div><cite>Title</cite> <span>Detail</span></div></li></ol>`). Recipes: an agenda that returns at each section break, with `aria-current` on the current item; a Q&A slide is a `closing` slide whose label says Questions. 174 175 **Transitions.** Default is a quick dissolve. `data-transition="push"`, `"move-in"` or `"none"` per slide (the incoming slide's setting wins). 176 177 **Magic Move.** Give an element on one slide and an element on the next the same `data-magic="id"` and they morph: position, size, colour, 178 opacity. If the typeface differs between the two (sentence to chip, serif to mono) it cross-fades while it travels. It works on text, boxes 179 and SVG; use a `<span>` rather than `<em>` for text that changes colour. A slide pair with no shared ids just dissolves. 180 181 ## 6. Diagrams that draw 182 183 Author the SVG with `viewBox="0 0 1680 H"` (so 1 unit is 1 px at full width) and use the engine classes so it follows the theme: 184 `dg-box` (outline), `dg-hot` (accent outline), `dg-line` and `dg-line hot`, `dg-dot`, text classes `dg-t` (label), `dg-s` (small), `dg-m` (mono), `dg-b` (accent). 185 Wrap groups in `<g data-build="fade" data-order="1">` for boxes and `<g data-build="draw" data-order="2">` for arrows (stroke-only paths, arrowheads as part of 186 the path). Crop the viewBox to the content (`viewBox="0 150 1680 330"`) so the diagram fills the slide. See `examples/src/gen_diagrams.py` for generators. 187 188 ## 6b. Images 189 190 Photos and illustrations go in `<img>` inside `image-left`, `image-right`, `team`, or as `data-bg` / `<img class="bleed">` on `full-bleed` (cropped with `object-fit: cover`, scrim added for legibility). 191 Always give `alt` text. Re-encode photos without EXIF/GPS (Pillow: open, convert, save; `sips` alone keeps metadata). 192 193 Local generation (nothing leaves the machine): `tools/gen-images.sh` renders the illustrations in `assets/` with the Draw Things CLI (`z_image_turbo`), strips metadata through Pillow and 194 writes JPEGs of about 70 to 110 KB; `tools/gen-images.sh name "prompt" seed WxH` renders one more. Rules that came from the Wireless 101 pipeline: generated images are **illustrative only**; never ask 195 for text, numbers, charts or diagrams (models garble them, so those stay SVG); no real people or brands; judge each render and drop the bad ones. 196 The four examples use `assets/aria-hero.jpg`, `aria-market.jpg` and `warehouse.jpg`; `abstract-teal.jpg` is a spare for dark decks. 197 198 ## 7. Presenter keys and tools 199 200 | Key | Action | 201 |---|---| 202 | right, down, space, PageDown, N, click | next build / slide | 203 | left, up, PageUp, Backspace, Shift+space | previous | 204 | Home / End | first / last slide | 205 | number + Enter | jump to slide (a toast shows what you typed; works in the presenter window too) | 206 | **G** | overview (light table; arrows move, Enter opens). **Esc** only closes panels, the overview, the laser or the marker; it never opens anything, so a clicker's Esc cannot put the grid on the projector | 207 | **P** | presenter view in a new window (this is the presenter view, not PDF export): current slide, a Next pane that previews the next build (or the next slide when builds are done), notes (A- / A+ or + / - change their size), timer (click or T pauses; `data-duration="20"` on the deck makes it a countdown that turns amber for the last two minutes), clock, an AUDIENCE SCREEN badge when the projector is blanked. Every key above works there too, and it reconnects if the audience window is reloaded (allow pop-ups) | 208 | **M** | marker: draw on the slide with mouse, pen or finger. **1 2 3 4** red / yellow / blue / white, **H** highlighter, **E** eraser, **Ctrl/Cmd+Z** undo, **C** clear, **Esc** leave. Kept per slide, remembered per deck in localStorage, shown in the presenter window, never printed | 209 | **L** | laser pointer: a red dot follows the mouse and leaves no trace | 210 | **O** | outline: every slide with title, link, layout, build count, notes flag; click to jump, filter, Copy as text; `#` copies one slide's link, Links copies them all | 211 | **K** | copy a link to this slide (also the link button in the toolbar) | 212 | **A** | narration on/off, when the deck has `data-narration` clips (see 12a) | 213 | **S** | theme and font panel; hover or focus a theme or pairing to preview it live on the slide, click to keep it | 214 | **B** or **.** / **W** | black / white screen | 215 | **F** or **F5** | fullscreen (F5 so a clicker's start button does not reload the page) | 216 217 The toolbar at the bottom fades when idle (and the cursor hides). Every slide has a link: `deck.html#pricing`, from `data-id="pricing"` on the section, else from its title, else `#slide-7` (`#/7` and `#7` work too); the address bar follows the current slide. Touch: swipe left/right; tap the 218 left 22% to go back (the rest advances); the toolbar stays visible while it has keyboard focus. `prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured in JS: no transitions, builds appear instantly, counters show the final value. 219 220 ## 8. PDF and print 221 222 Open the deck in Chrome, **Cmd/Ctrl+P**, destination "Save as PDF", margins "None", turn on "Background graphics". `@page` is 1920x1080 px, one slide per 223 page, all builds shown, backgrounds kept, toolbar and marker hidden. Headless: `page.pdf({preferCSSPageSize: true, printBackground: true})`. 224 225 ## 9. Right-to-left and Arabic 226 227 Set `dir="rtl" lang="ar"` on `<html>` (the lang drives chart number formatting: Arabic-Indic digits for `ar`, and `data-build="count"` accepts Arabic-Indic digits) or on a single `<section>`. See `examples/arabic-sample.html`. Serif themes carry `--f-ar-d` (Noto Naskh Arabic) for Arabic headings; Arabic headings get line-height 1.25. All layout uses logical properties, so slides mirror (image-left becomes right, timelines run 228 right to left, the wipe direction flips). An Arabic face loads on demand. Keep code in `dir="ltr"` blocks (the code layout already is). 229 230 ## 10. Checker 231 232 ``` 233 node check.mjs deck.html [more.html] [--themes] [--shots out/] [--outline] 234 ``` 235 236 Opens each deck at 1920x1080, shows every slide with all builds revealed and prints a short list: `slide n: element, what is wrong, fix:`. It reports 237 content outside the safe area (120 px sides, 96 px top/bottom) or the slide, text wider than its box, text under 20 px, text contrast under 4.5:1 (including 238 gradient-filled headline accents), and console errors. Exit code 1 on failure; a 15-slide deck takes about 2 seconds. `--themes` repeats the run in every 239 theme the deck defines (use it before sending a deck to someone who might press S). `--shots` saves a PNG per slide. `--outline` prints the deck's outline (n, title, layout, builds, magic, and `NO NOTES` where notes are missing), handy for reviewing a generated deck without opening it. 240 241 Needs Playwright: `npm i playwright && npx playwright install chromium`. Or set `PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE=/path/to/playwright/index.mjs` and 242 `CHROME_PATH=/path/to/chrome`. 243 244 ## 12. Checklist before you present 245 246 - `node check.mjs deck.html --themes` is green. 247 - Press **G**: the sequence reads as a story; every slide has one claim. 248 - Press **P**: notes on every slide that needs one; the timer works. 249 - Try the Magic Move pairs and the builds once in presentation order. 250 - Print to PDF and look at page 1, the chart page and the last page. 251 - Open with the system's reduced-motion setting on if your audience may need it. 252 253 ## 12a. Narration (recorded voice per slide) 254 255 Add `data-narration="audio/my-deck/"` to `<main class="deck">` and put one MP3 per slide in that folder, named after the 256 slide's link id (`data-id`, for example `audio/my-deck/pricing.mp3`). A speaker button appears in the toolbar once the first 257 slide's clip loads (key **A**, also from the presenter window). While narration is on, each slide plays its clip, shows all 258 its builds, and moves to the next slide when the clip ends; navigating by hand keeps narrating from where you land. 259 Until the files exist the deck shows no button at all, so a deck can ship first and get its voice later. 260 261 ## 12b. Slides that run 262 263 A slide is a web page, so it can hold things a slide file can't: a working app screen, a calculator, a simulation you drag, 264 sound and speech, code you edit and run, a game, another page in an iframe, a video that plays only on its slide, a live camera. 265 `examples/beyond-slides.html` has one of each; its source (`examples/src/beyond-slides.html`) is the pattern to copy: 266 wrap widgets in `.bx-ui` (clicks there don't advance), take colours from the theme tokens, and run anything that moves or 267 makes sound only while the slide is current. The video in it (`assets/edit-in-browser.mp4`) is a recording of `editor.html`. 268 269 ## 13. Known limits 270 271 - Web fonts come from Google Fonts on demand; offline, the system fallbacks in each stack are used (set `data-fonts="system"` for fully offline decks). 272 - Charts are simple on purpose: column, bar and line, up to three series, no stacked or dual-axis. 273 - Magic Move morphs matching elements; it does not morph SVG path shapes into different paths. 274 - The presenter view needs pop-ups allowed and uses `postMessage`, so both windows must stay open. 275 - The engine fits type by shrinking to 78% (display numbers and headlines to 50%); below that the checker reports the slide instead of shrinking further. 276 277 <!-- LIBRARY:START (generated by tools/build-gallery.mjs from tools/library-data.mjs; edit the data file) --> 278

file.content: # Keynote Pro manual (the engine behind present-in-html) Paths below are the engine's. In this skill: `check.mjs` and `tools/*.mjs` are in `scripts/`; `template.html`, `library/` and `examples/` are in `assets/`. Build tools and the sample decks mentioned here are not shipped with the skill. - 1. Write a deck in 60 seconds - 2. Layout cheat-sheet (shortest working snippet for each) - 3. Deck recipes (theme, fonts, sequence, builds) - 4. Theme design plans (DESIGN.md format) - 5. Builds, transitions, Magic Move - 6. Diagrams that draw - 6b. Images - 7. Presenter keys and tools - 8. PDF and print - 9. Right-to-left and Arabic - 10. Checker - 12. Checklist before you present - 12a. Narration (recorded voice per slide) - 12b. Slides that run - 13. Known limits ## 1. Write a deck in 60 seconds 1. Copy `template.html`. Set `data-theme` (and optionally `data-fonts`) on ``, and the title in `` and `data-title` on `<main class="deck">`. 2. Delete the sample slides. Add `<section class="slide" data-layout="...">` blocks (cheat-sheet below). 3. Add `<aside class="notes"><p>...</p></aside>` inside any slide for presenter notes. 4. `node check.mjs my-deck.html`, fix what it lists, open it, press **P**. Rules of thumb: one idea per slide; at most 5 bullets; say the number, not the paragraph. Layouts auto-fit (type shrinks to 78% before content would leave the safe area, and short content grows, up to 1.25x on bullets and 1.5x on statements, so a slide is never half empty), lists balance their wrapping, images crop with `object-fit: cover`. You never tune CSS to make text fit; if `check.mjs` still complains, cut words. ## 2. Layout cheat-sheet (shortest working snippet for each) Every snippet goes inside `<section class="slide" data-layout="NAME"> ... </section>`. <figcaption>Source</figcaption> --> <!-- comparison --> <h2>Title</h2><table><thead><tr><th></th><th>A</th><th class="rec" data-tag="Recommended">B</th></tr></thead> <tbody><tr><th>Price</th><td>$1</td><td>$2</td></tr></tbody></table> <!-- timeline --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="timeline" data-build="list"><li><time>Q1</time><h3>Step</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- class="now" marks today --> <!-- process --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="steps" data-build="list"><li><h3>Capture</h3><p>Detail</p></li>...</ol> <!-- 3 to 5 steps --> <!-- quote --> <blockquote>The quote with an <em>accent</em>.</blockquote><cite><b>Name</b>Title, Company</cite> <!-- code --> <h2>Title</h2><pre data-lang="js" data-focus="1-2;4-6;*"> code </pre> <!-- indent freely; 2 to 4 vitals; timed course. data-flag marks an abnormal value --> <!-- ask --> <h2>Raising a seed round</h2><div class="amount"><b data-build="count">$2.5<small>M</small></b><span>What it buys</span></div> <ul class="use"><li style="--w:50"><b>Engineering</b><span>50%</span><i></i></li></ul><dl class="terms"><div><dt>Instrument</dt><dd>SAFE</dd></div></dl> <!-- rows --> <h2>Title</h2><ol class="rows"><li data-k="Issue"><p>Text</p></li><li data-k="Conclusion" data-hot><h3>Bold line</h3><p>Text</p></li></ol> <!-- labelled rows: issue / rule / application / conclusion; situation / complication / resolution; claim / evidence / caveat. data-hot highlights one --> <!-- quiz --> <h2>Question?</h2><ol class="opts" data-build="reveal"><li>A</li><li data-correct>B</li><li>C</li><li>D</li></ol> <!-- the click marks the data-correct option --> <!-- materials --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="board"><figure class="mat" style="--sw:#9a9892"><figcaption><b>Concrete</b><span>Where it goes</span></figcaption></figure>...</div> <!-- or an <img> in each figure; --tx adds a texture gradient --> <!-- formula --> <h2>Title</h2><div class="eq"><i>P<sub>r</sub></i> = <i>P<sub>t</sub></i> − <span class="hot"><i>L</i></span></div><dl class="terms"><div><dt><i>P<sub>t</sub></i></dt><dd>Meaning</dd></div></dl> <!-- two-column x3 -> add data-cols="3" to the section for three columns (now / next / later) --> <!-- closing --> <h2>Thank you</h2><p class="contact"><span><b>Web</b> example.com</span><span>me@example.com</span></p> ``` Extras: `<p class="label">` is the small mono kicker above a title (use it on some slides, not all). `.chip` is a boxed token; `.chip.hot` highlights one. `.lede`, `.src` and `<small>` are secondary text. `data-footer="off"` hides the footer, `data-fit="off"` stops auto-fit, `data-tone="hero"` (or `"plain"`) swaps a slide into (or out of) the theme's hero palette. ## 3. Deck recipes (theme, fonts, sequence, builds) Fonts: `data-fonts` is optional; leave it empty to use the theme's own pairing. | Need | Theme | Sequence of layouts | Builds | |---|---|---|---| | **Product launch** | `keynote-black` (cinematic) or `keynote-white` | title, statement, statement + big-number (Magic Move on the number), stats, full-bleed, image-left, chart or comparison, quote, timeline, closing | `count` on stats, `list` on timeline, magic on the hero number | | **Quarterly / board review** | `boardroom` | title, agenda, big-number, chart (actual vs plan), stats, chart (line with `data-min`), section, comparison (mark `rec`), two-column (risks / mitigations), timeline, bullets (decisions), closing | `count` on KPIs, `draw` on charts, `list` on decisions | | **Tech talk** | `swiss` (or `studio`) | title, statement + big-number (problem), diagram (before), section, diagram (after), process, code (`data-focus`), chart (line), comparison, two-column (worked / didn't), stats, closing | `draw` + `fade` on diagram groups, focus on code | | **Training / course** | `studio` (or `editorial`) | title, agenda, statement, diagrams, process, big-number, chart, comparison, code, quote, timeline (where we are), closing | `list`, `draw`, one `count` | | **Investor pitch** | `keynote-white` + `data-fonts="grotesk"` | title, statement (problem), big-number (market), image-left (solution), stats (traction), chart (growth), comparison (vs alternatives), team, timeline (use of funds), closing | `count` on traction, `draw` on the growth chart | | **Weekly status update** | `editorial` or `keynote-white` | title, bullets (done), stats (health), chart (trend), timeline (next), two-column (risks / asks), closing | `list` only; keep it quiet | Authoring order that works in one pass: write the title and the one-sentence story, pick the recipe, write each slide's single claim as its `<h2>`, then add the supporting snippet, then notes, then run `check.mjs`. ## 4. Theme design plans (DESIGN.md format) Each theme is a real, shippable look. One accent, hairline rules, big type. All body text is at least 4.5:1. ### keynote-white - **Overview.** Apple-clean. Mostly white, enormous tightly-tracked headlines, one blue phrase per slide. Fits launches, pitches, status decks. - **Colors.** bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f5f5f7`, ink `#1d1d1f`, ink2 `#5f5f64`, rule `#d2d2d7`, brand `#0066cc` (on-brand `#fff`), hero = same as page. - **Typography.** Display and body Inter (700 display, -0.035em), mono JetBrains Mono for labels and code. - **Shape.** Radius 14 px (panels), 6 px bars, 1 px rules. - **Signature.** Whitespace and scale; the accent `<em>` is the only colour on a title. - **Do / Don't.** Do keep slides sparse. Don't add boxes around everything. ### keynote-black - **Overview.** Cinematic dark for reveals and demos; the same system on pure black. - **Colors.** bg `#000`, surface `#161618`, ink `#f5f5f7`, ink2 `#a1a1a6`, rule `#38383a`, brand `#2997ff`, em gradient `#2997ff` to `#c58bff`. - **Typography.** Inter 700 display; JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** 14 px radius, 6 px bars. - **Signature.** Gradient-filled headline accent, the only gradient in the system. Code panel `#1c1c1e` with Xcode-dark colours. - **Do / Don't.** Do use for rooms with dim light. Don't print it (use keynote-white for PDF handouts). ### boardroom - **Overview.** PowerPoint-corporate done well: navy, serif titles, gold accent, rules above the footer. - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#eef1f6`, ink `#0b2545`, ink2 `#46576f`, rule `#c8d0dc`, brand `#c19a3d` (text version `#7a5a0a`); hero bg navy `#0b2545` with gold `#e2b658`. - **Typography.** Source Serif 4 (600) titles, Source Sans 3 body, JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** 2 px radius, square bars, 1 px rules. - **Signature.** Gold spine on title and closing slides; gold left bar on every title; navy code panel. - **Do / Don't.** Do put the decision on the last slide. Don't use more than one chart per slide. ### swiss - **Overview.** International typographic style: hard grid, black rules, one red. - **Colors.** bg `#fff`, surface `#f0f0f0`, ink `#111`, ink2 `#555`, rule `#cfcfcf`, strong rule `#111`, brand `#d7000f`; hero slides are solid red with white type. - **Typography.** Inter Tight 700 (-0.03em) display, Inter body, JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** Zero radius everywhere, 2 px black rule above the footer. - **Signature.** A 96x20 red tab on the top margin and full-red hero slides. - **Do / Don't.** Do align everything to the grid. Don't round corners. ### editorial - **Overview.** A printed essay: paper, ink, oxblood, italic emphasis. - **Colors.** bg `#f4efe6`, surface `#ebe4d6`, ink `#1c1a17`, ink2 `#5a5347`, rule `#cfc5b2`, brand `#8f2d17`; hero is ink `#1c1a17` with terracotta `#e49467`. - **Typography.** Newsreader 400 display (italic for `<em>`), Inter body, JetBrains Mono. - **Shape.** Zero radius, 1 px rules. - **Signature.** A masthead double rule across the top of every slide. - **Do / Don't.** Do write full sentences as titles. Don't use all-caps. ### studio - **Overview.** Deep teal and amber, the look of the Wireless 101 courses: for teaching and talks. - **Colors.** bg `#0a2a2f`, surface `#0f3a40`, ink `#efe8d8`, ink2 `#a9c0bd`, rule `#2c5a5f`, brand `#f0a93b` (on-brand `#0a2a2f`); hero `#061c20`. - **Typography.** Instrument Serif display (italic amber `<em>`), DM Sans body, Space Mono labels. - **Shape.** 4 px radius, 2 px bars. - **Signature.** An amber dot starts every label. - **Do / Don't.** Do keep diagrams to the amber and cream. Don't add a second accent. Press **S** in any deck to switch theme and font pairing live; hovering an option previews it on the slide, a click keeps it (remembered per deck in localStorage). **Font library** (9 core pairings below live in the template; the profession pairings live in `library/fonts/` and are copied into a deck with `tools/add-look.mjs`. The settings panel groups them as Core and Library, and picking a library theme selects its own pairing; `fonts.html` shows them all as specimens with your own headline): Inter (neo-grotesk), Sora/Inter (geometric), Space Grotesk/Inter (grotesk with character), IBM Plex Sans/Plex Mono (technical), Fraunces/Inter, Playfair/Source Sans, Spectral/Public Sans, Cormorant Garamond/Source Sans (set at 1.15x via `--display-scale`), and system fonts. Type sizes come from one scale: `--t-display --t-h1 --t-h2 --t-h3 --t-body --t-small` (164/132/84/48/36/28 px; 28 px is the floor for anything the audience reads). Set one with `data-fonts="sora"` on `<html>`. To recolour any theme, add one line: `html{--brand:#7c3aed;--brand-text:#7c3aed}`. ## 5. Builds, transitions, Magic Move **Builds** reveal parts of a slide one click at a time. Right arrow / space / click reveals the next build, then the next slide; left steps back. | Attribute | Effect | |---|---| | `data-build="fade"`, `rise`, `scale`, `wipe` | the element appears | | `data-build="list"` on a `ul`/`ol` | children appear one by one (`data-item="fade"` to change the style) | | `data-build="draw"` on an SVG shape or `<g>` | strokes draw themselves (every shape inside is staggered) | | `data-build="count"` | the number counts up from 0 (`$4.2M`, `38.4%`, `1,840` all work); markup holds the final value | | `data-build="draw"` on a chart figure | bars grow, lines draw, labels arrive | | `data-focus="1-3;5-7;*"` on a `pre` | each click lights the next range of lines (`*` = all) | | `data-order="2"` | builds with the same order arrive together; give all builds an order or none | | `data-delay="200"` | extra delay in ms | Print, overview thumbnails and `check.mjs` always show every build; the presenter window's Next pane shows the next one. Charts take `data-target="200"` (a dashed target line), `data-delta="pct"` or `"abs"` (a delta label on two-series columns), `data-muted="2"` (which series is the muted reference; with two bar series the second is one by default, `data-equal` turns that off) and `data-highlight` (also on line charts). Chart data is exposed to screen readers as a hidden table. Use builds where order matters; most slides need none. **Skip, appendix and the end.** `data-skip` on a slide keeps it in the overview, outline and PDF but jumps over it in play (Keynote's Skip Slide); use it for backup slides. A slide with `data-layout="appendix"` renders as a section divider and it and every slide after it are skipped in play. Pressing next on the last slide shows an "End of show" screen (`data-end="off"` on the deck turns it off). Cite sources with `<sup class="cite">[1]</sup>` and list them on a `references` slide (`<ol class="refs"><li><div><cite>Title</cite> <span>Detail</span></div></li></ol>`). Recipes: an agenda that returns at each section break, with `aria-current` on the current item; a Q&A slide is a `closing` slide whose label says Questions. **Transitions.** Default is a quick dissolve. `data-transition="push"`, `"move-in"` or `"none"` per slide (the incoming slide's setting wins). **Magic Move.** Give an element on one slide and an element on the next the same `data-magic="id"` and they morph: position, size, colour, opacity. If the typeface differs between the two (sentence to chip, serif to mono) it cross-fades while it travels. It works on text, boxes and SVG; use a `<span>` rather than `<em>` for text that changes colour. A slide pair with no shared ids just dissolves. ## 6. Diagrams that draw Author the SVG with `viewBox="0 0 1680 H"` (so 1 unit is 1 px at full width) and use the engine classes so it follows the theme: `dg-box` (outline), `dg-hot` (accent outline), `dg-line` and `dg-line hot`, `dg-dot`, text classes `dg-t` (label), `dg-s` (small), `dg-m` (mono), `dg-b` (accent). Wrap groups in `<g data-build="fade" data-order="1">` for boxes and `<g data-build="draw" data-order="2">` for arrows (stroke-only paths, arrowheads as part of the path). Crop the viewBox to the content (`viewBox="0 150 1680 330"`) so the diagram fills the slide. See `examples/src/gen_diagrams.py` for generators. ## 6b. Images Photos and illustrations go in `<img>` inside `image-left`, `image-right`, `team`, or as `data-bg` / `<img class="bleed">` on `full-bleed` (cropped with `object-fit: cover`, scrim added for legibility). Always give `alt` text. Re-encode photos without EXIF/GPS (Pillow: open, convert, save; `sips` alone keeps metadata). Local generation (nothing leaves the machine): `tools/gen-images.sh` renders the illustrations in `assets/` with the Draw Things CLI (`z_image_turbo`), strips metadata through Pillow and writes JPEGs of about 70 to 110 KB; `tools/gen-images.sh name "prompt" seed WxH` renders one more. Rules that came from the Wireless 101 pipeline: generated images are **illustrative only**; never ask for text, numbers, charts or diagrams (models garble them, so those stay SVG); no real people or brands; judge each render and drop the bad ones. The four examples use `assets/aria-hero.jpg`, `aria-market.jpg` and `warehouse.jpg`; `abstract-teal.jpg` is a spare for dark decks. ## 7. Presenter keys and tools | Key | Action | |---|---| | right, down, space, PageDown, N, click | next build / slide | | left, up, PageUp, Backspace, Shift+space | previous | | Home / End | first / last slide | | number + Enter | jump to slide (a toast shows what you typed; works in the presenter window too) | | **G** | overview (light table; arrows move, Enter opens). **Esc** only closes panels, the overview, the laser or the marker; it never opens anything, so a clicker's Esc cannot put the grid on the projector | | **P** | presenter view in a new window (this is the presenter view, not PDF export): current slide, a Next pane that previews the next build (or the next slide when builds are done), notes (A- / A+ or + / - change their size), timer (click or T pauses; `data-duration="20"` on the deck makes it a countdown that turns amber for the last two minutes), clock, an AUDIENCE SCREEN badge when the projector is blanked. Every key above works there too, and it reconnects if the audience window is reloaded (allow pop-ups) | | **M** | marker: draw on the slide with mouse, pen or finger. **1 2 3 4** red / yellow / blue / white, **H** highlighter, **E** eraser, **Ctrl/Cmd+Z** undo, **C** clear, **Esc** leave. Kept per slide, remembered per deck in localStorage, shown in the presenter window, never printed | | **L** | laser pointer: a red dot follows the mouse and leaves no trace | | **O** | outline: every slide with title, link, layout, build count, notes flag; click to jump, filter, Copy as text; `#` copies one slide's link, Links copies them all | | **K** | copy a link to this slide (also the link button in the toolbar) | | **A** | narration on/off, when the deck has `data-narration` clips (see 12a) | | **S** | theme and font panel; hover or focus a theme or pairing to preview it live on the slide, click to keep it | | **B** or **.** / **W** | black / white screen | | **F** or **F5** | fullscreen (F5 so a clicker's start button does not reload the page) | The toolbar at the bottom fades when idle (and the cursor hides). Every slide has a link: `deck.html#pricing`, from `data-id="pricing"` on the section, else from its title, else `#slide-7` (`#/7` and `#7` work too); the address bar follows the current slide. Touch: swipe left/right; tap the left 22% to go back (the rest advances); the toolbar stays visible while it has keyboard focus. `prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured in JS: no transitions, builds appear instantly, counters show the final value. ## 8. PDF and print Open the deck in Chrome, **Cmd/Ctrl+P**, destination "Save as PDF", margins "None", turn on "Background graphics". `@page` is 1920x1080 px, one slide per page, all builds shown, backgrounds kept, toolbar and marker hidden. Headless: `page.pdf({preferCSSPageSize: true, printBackground: true})`. ## 9. Right-to-left and Arabic Set `dir="rtl" lang="ar"` on `<html>` (the lang drives chart number formatting: Arabic-Indic digits for `ar`, and `data-build="count"` accepts Arabic-Indic digits) or on a single `<section>`. See `examples/arabic-sample.html`. Serif themes carry `--f-ar-d` (Noto Naskh Arabic) for Arabic headings; Arabic headings get line-height 1.25. All layout uses logical properties, so slides mirror (image-left becomes right, timelines run right to left, the wipe direction flips). An Arabic face loads on demand. Keep code in `dir="ltr"` blocks (the code layout already is). ## 10. Checker ``` node check.mjs deck.html [more.html] [--themes] [--shots out/] [--outline] ``` Opens each deck at 1920x1080, shows every slide with all builds revealed and prints a short list: `slide n: element, what is wrong, fix:`. It reports content outside the safe area (120 px sides, 96 px top/bottom) or the slide, text wider than its box, text under 20 px, text contrast under 4.5:1 (including gradient-filled headline accents), and console errors. Exit code 1 on failure; a 15-slide deck takes about 2 seconds. `--themes` repeats the run in every theme the deck defines (use it before sending a deck to someone who might press S). `--shots` saves a PNG per slide. `--outline` prints the deck's outline (n, title, layout, builds, magic, and `NO NOTES` where notes are missing), handy for reviewing a generated deck without opening it. Needs Playwright: `npm i playwright && npx playwright install chromium`. Or set `PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE=/path/to/playwright/index.mjs` and `CHROME_PATH=/path/to/chrome`. ## 12. Checklist before you present - `node check.mjs deck.html --themes` is green. - Press **G**: the sequence reads as a story; every slide has one claim. - Press **P**: notes on every slide that needs one; the timer works. - Try the Magic Move pairs and the builds once in presentation order. - Print to PDF and look at page 1, the chart page and the last page. - Open with the system's reduced-motion setting on if your audience may need it. ## 12a. Narration (recorded voice per slide) Add `data-narration="audio/my-deck/"` to `<main class="deck">` and put one MP3 per slide in that folder, named after the slide's link id (`data-id`, for example `audio/my-deck/pricing.mp3`). A speaker button appears in the toolbar once the first slide's clip loads (key **A**, also from the presenter window). While narration is on, each slide plays its clip, shows all its builds, and moves to the next slide when the clip ends; navigating by hand keeps narrating from where you land. Until the files exist the deck shows no button at all, so a deck can ship first and get its voice later. ## 12b. Slides that run A slide is a web page, so it can hold things a slide file can't: a working app screen, a calculator, a simulation you drag, sound and speech, code you edit and run, a game, another page in an iframe, a video that plays only on its slide, a live camera. `examples/beyond-slides.html` has one of each; its source (`examples/src/beyond-slides.html`) is the pattern to copy: wrap widgets in `.bx-ui` (clicks there don't advance), take colours from the theme tokens, and run anything that moves or makes sound only while the slide is current. The video in it (`assets/edit-in-browser.mp4`) is a recording of `editor.html`. ## 13. Known limits - Web fonts come from Google Fonts on demand; offline, the system fallbacks in each stack are used (set `data-fonts="system"` for fully offline decks). - Charts are simple on purpose: column, bar and line, up to three series, no stacked or dual-axis. - Magic Move morphs matching elements; it does not morph SVG path shapes into different paths. - The presenter view needs pop-ups allowed and uses `postMessage`, so both windows must stay open. - The engine fits type by shrinking to 78% (display numbers and headlines to 50%); below that the checker reports the slide instead of shrinking further. <!-- LIBRARY:START (generated by tools/build-gallery.mjs from tools/library-data.mjs; edit the data file) -->

1	# Engine notes (read when the deck needs one of these)
2	
3	Contents: slide links · live demos on slides · narration · `window.kp` API · slide attributes · old decks
4	
5	## Slide links
6	
7	Every slide has its own address: `my-deck.html#pricing`. It comes from `data-id="pricing"` on the `<section>`, otherwise from
8	the slide title, otherwise `#slide-7` (`#/7` and `#7` also work). Set `data-id` on slides people will link to (the ask, the
9	pricing, the demo) and keep ids short, lowercase, unique and stable across edits, because links already shared depend on them.
10	**K** copies the current slide's link; the outline (**O**) has a `#` per slide and "Links" copies them all.
11	
12	## Slides that run: live demos on a slide
13	
14	When a live demo beats a picture (product UI, calculator, simulation, sound, code to edit, a game, an embedded page, video,
15	camera), build it on the slide. `assets/examples/beyond-slides.html` has one working pattern for each; copy from it.
16	What those patterns get right, and why:
17	- Slide: `data-layout="two-column" data-fit="off" data-demo`, a `.col.bx-text` (label, h2, short text) and a `.col.bx-stage.bx-ui`.
18	- Wrap widgets in `.bx-ui` and stop `click` there, or every click inside the demo advances the deck. Text inputs stop
19	  `keydown` and blur on Enter/Escape, so typing does not trigger deck shortcuts.
20	- Colours come from theme tokens (`getComputedStyle(slide).getPropertyValue('--brand')` for canvas), re-read on slide enter,
21	  so pressing **S** restyles demos too.
22	- Animate, play sound, video or camera only while the slide has `.is-current` (watch its class with a MutationObserver) and stop
23	  on leave; otherwise a hidden slide burns CPU or keeps talking. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Load iframes on enter
24	  (`data-src`). Camera and sound start from a button, never on their own.
25	- Text in widgets stays at 28px or more (the checker's floor). Wait for `window.kp.ready` before wiring.
26	
27	## Narration
28	
29	`<main class="deck" data-narration="audio/my-deck/">` plays `<folder>/<slide link id>.mp3` per slide (key **A** or the speaker
30	button, which stays hidden until the first slide's clip exists, so a deck can ship before its audio). While on, each slide
31	plays its clip, reveals its builds and advances when the clip ends; a slide without a clip shows a note and moves on after 3 s.
32	Write one transcript per slide and name clips by `data-id`.
33	
34	## `window.kp` (after `kp.ready`)
35	
36	`go(i, step)`, `next()`, `prev()`, `showAll(i)`, `refit()`, `outline()`, `count`, `state`, `slugs`, `link(i)`, `copyLink(i)`,
37	`applyLook(theme, fonts, persist, preview)` (fonts `''` = the theme's own), `themes`, `fonts` (id lists). The registry is read
38	from the marker comments in `<style id="kp-themes">`.
39	
40	## Slide attributes and small facts
41	
42	- Layouts (`data-layout`): agenda, appendix, ask, big-number, bullets, case, chart, closing, code, comparison, diagram, formula,
